items.title: Effect in routine general practice is uncertain
items.whyItMatters: The most applicable trial's interval crosses zero (claim c2), so expansion could bring little benefit.
items.opportunity: A randomised comparison powered for a patient-relevant HbA1c difference.

items.title: Attenders are not comparable with non-attenders
items.whyItMatters: Existing records would overstate benefit because attenders differ (claim c3).
items.opportunity: Randomise eligible patients rather than compare those who chose groups.

items.title: Who cannot take part
items.whyItMatters: Patients with limited English or shift work attend least (claim c4).
items.opportunity: Offer evening sessions and interpreting, and report attendance by work status and language.

items.title: Patient-reported outcomes rarely measured
items.whyItMatters: Distress and confidence may improve even when HbA1c changes little.
items.opportunity: Include diabetes distress as a secondary outcome.

errorsFound: 'People seem to like them' describes attenders, a self-selected group; it is not evidence that group visits work better.
reevaluation: The question needs a randomised comparison of group visits with individual reviews in general practice, with attendance and equity measured.
summary: Four gaps; uncertain effect in general practice and self-selection are high severity.
